tldr: In reward models for robot reinforcement learning, RynnValue is proposed as a value foundation model that replaces conventional preferences and normalized progress with temporal distance (directed cost-to-go) derived from timestamps. Trained on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous data without pairwise preference annotations, it significantly improves trajectory evaluation in unseen environments and boosts real-world reinforcement learning success rates.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of RynnValue. Given language instructions and multimodal image sequences, it predicts the absolute remaining time to task completion and relative temporal differences across observations via grouped temporal queries. It is also structured to concurrently generate natural language descriptions of video content and task success/failure judgments.
overview:
When robots acquire diverse skills via reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck lies in how to provide general-purpose reward signals. Handcrafted reward functions are difficult to design, and sparse success-only rewards cannot guide learning in long-horizon tasks. While pretrained reward models have drawn growing attention, conventional methods rely on human pairwise preferences or trajectory progress normalized between 0 and 1. These targets struggle to stay consistent across differing robot embodiments and task durations, making scaling to large datasets challenging.

To overcome this, the authors rethink the supervisory target. Instead of predicting a relative trajectory score, they introduce RynnValue, a value foundation model that directly predicts the directed cost-to-go from the current state to the language-specified goal—that is, temporal distance. Since temporal distance labels can be derived automatically from timestamps once the video completion cutoff is known, diverse datasets can be unified without expensive human annotations.

The authors scale this approach across more than 7,000 hours of video (roughly 3 million instruction-conditioned clips) spanning single-arm, bimanual, mobile, dexterous, simulation, and first-person human data. To prevent the model from exploiting shortcuts such as frame ordering or sampling intervals, they incorporate techniques like temporal-order shuffling and value-isolation attention.

In evaluations on unseen trajectory ranking, RynnValue outperforms fully preference-supervised state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, when converted into dense rewards for real-world bimanual robot RL, it substantially improves success rates from 63.8% to 82.5% in offline RL and from 52.5% to 72.5% in online RL.
contributions: Redefines the supervisory target for reward models from conventional preferences or normalized progress to temporal distance (cost-to-go), unifying heterogeneous robot data under a single physical metric.

Establishes a low-cost scaling recipe that constructs a massive dataset of over 7,000 hours and roughly 3 million clips using only video timestamps and automated subtask cutoffs, without any human preference annotations.
Introduces temporal-order shuffling and Value-Isolation Attention, suppressing shortcut learning based on presentation order or neighboring values to ground predictions purely on visual evidence.
Achieves state-of-the-art ranking performance on unseen robots and environments, and delivers substantial success rate gains in both online and offline RL on real dual-arm robots.

sections.heading: Why temporal distance instead of normalized progress?
sections.summary: The main bottleneck in scaling robot reinforcement learning is designing general-purpose reward functions. Because conventional preference labels and normalized [0, 1] progress do not transfer cleanly across heterogeneous data, this work proposes temporal distance to task completion, readily derived from timestamps, as a unified value interface.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning is increasingly adopted in robot learning, but the real bottleneck is how to specify rewards rather than policy expressiveness. Handcrafting reward functions fails on open-ended tasks, and sparse rewards that give a 1 only upon success make learning long-horizon tasks intractable.

Existing general-purpose reward models have relied on pairwise preferences between trajectories or progress normalized to $[0, 1]$ over an episode. However, what progress 0.5 means varies widely depending on execution speed and task steps. This is fundamentally different from cost-to-go in optimal control, making it extremely difficult to aggregate data across different robots and environments.

This work advocates shifting from reward models that score trajectory quality to value foundation models that predict the directed temporal cost-to-go toward a language-specified goal. Under minimum-time optimal control, the remaining time to the goal serves as the natural value function. Moreover, once the completion timestamp of a clip is identified, supervision can be generated simply by subtracting timestamps, completely removing the need for human comparative labels.

However, naively training a model with multiple image frames allows it to exploit spurious shortcuts—such as assuming frames are evenly spaced or that later frames are inevitably closer to the goal—making it blind to task failures and regressions. RynnValue achieves robust value learning grounded purely in images and task instructions by combining random temporal sampling, temporal-order shuffling, and an attention mechanism that prevents information leakage across queries.

sections.heading: Grouped temporal queries and isolating attention to stop cheating
sections.summary: Built on the multimodal foundation model RynnBrain, RynnValue simultaneously predicts absolute time-to-go and relative temporal differences from image sequences. Its core design features multi-token grouped queries, a distributional readout head for continuous time, and Value-Isolation Attention to prevent query cheating.
sections.details:
RynnValue's architecture takes a language instruction $\ell$, robot metadata $m$, and $K=8$ sampled observation images $\mathcal{I}$, outputting absolute temporal distance for each image and relative temporal differences between adjacent images.

Key architectural designs include:

- **Grouped temporal queries**:
  Reading object placement, robot contact states, and intermediate phases from a single image creates an informational bottleneck for a single token. The method assigns $N=8$ tokens to each absolute query $\mathbf{V}_i$ and relative query $\mathbf{R}_i$. After interacting through bidirectional attention, they are concatenated along the feature dimension to form rich representations.

- **Continuous temporal readouts via distributional heads**:
  The regression over absolute time (0 to 512 s) and relative time (-256 to +256 s) is framed as a classification problem over 256 bins in symlog space (a scale-compressing transform), using two-hot target representations that split probability between the two nearest bins. This avoids gradient instability caused by wide target scales and stabilizes training.

- **Value-Isolation Attention to prevent shortcuts**:
  If value queries across different frames can attend to one another, the model can simply interpolate a smooth curve from surrounding queries, ignoring robot mistakes or setbacks. The model masks cross-observation query attention entirely, forcing each query to base its prediction solely on its corresponding image and task instruction.

- **Natural language video analysis and verification**:
  Beyond temporal predictions, the native language model head autoregressively generates textual descriptions of the video, task alignment checks, and success/failure judgments. This enhances both interpretability and vision-language representation alignment.

Multi-token absolute and relative temporal queries are inserted alongside input image sequences, outputting continuous time estimates through distributional heads while autoregressively generating natural language scene descriptions and task verification from a terminal prompt.

sections.heading: Turning timestamps into supervision and shaping RL rewards
sections.summary: Remaining-time labels are generated automatically from timestamps across more than 7,000 hours of heterogeneous data. During training, robustness is enforced through temporal-order shuffling and instruction mismatching; at inference time, predictions are transformed into RL rewards via potential-based reward shaping.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Data Preparation and Labeling
The training corpus consolidates diverse sources (roughly 1.67M raw episodes), including single-arm, dual-arm, mobile manipulators, dexterous hands, simulators, and first-person human demonstrations. By segmenting these into subtasks and re-anchoring completion cutoffs, the authors create approximately 3 million instruction-conditioned clips.

The key advantage is that ground truth for each frame is simply defined as cut-off timestamp minus current frame timestamp. This eliminates the need to calibrate or normalize progress scales across heterogeneous datasets.

### 3.2 Training Recipe to Suppress Shortcuts
When feeding multi-frame inputs to visual models, networks easily overfit to non-visual structural patterns. The recipe includes:

- **Random temporal sampling**: Sampling 8 frames at random timestamps rather than uniform intervals removes the shortcut of inferring time from frame spacing.
- **Temporal-order shuffling**: Deliberately rearranging the input sequence order (Figure F2(a) B). Half the batches are fully shuffled, and the other half follow random walks with occasional reversals, preventing the assumption that later frames must be closer to the goal.
- **Instruction mismatch augmentation**: Injecting unrelated task instructions 10% of the time to teach the model how to detect mismatched video-language pairs. Absolute time losses are masked during mismatches, optimizing only relative predictions and the text output indicating a mismatch.

### 3.3 Inference and RL Reward Interface
During inference, frames are processed in chronological order. The predicted temporal distance $v_t$ (remaining seconds) is non-negative, but RL policies benefit from higher values near the goal. The authors define potential as $\Phi_t = -v_t$. Using potential-based reward shaping, dense feedback is provided to the policy via $R_t = r_{\mathrm{sparse}} + \kappa (\gamma \Phi_{t} - \Phi_{t-1})$.

captions.F2: Training strategies and Value-Isolation Attention structure. (a) shows random sampling, temporal-order shuffling, and instruction mismatch augmentation, while (b) displays the attention mask blocking direct cross-frame attention between value queries.

sections.heading: Superior ranking accuracy on benchmarks and real-world RL gains
sections.summary: On out-of-domain trajectory ranking (RBM-EVAL-OOD), RynnValue reaches Kendall’s $\tau_a = 0.675$ without any preference supervision, outperforming preference-trained state-of-the-art models. In real bimanual RL experiments, it yields major success rate improvements over competitive baselines.
sections.details:
### 4.1–4.2 Benchmark Evaluation (RBM-EVAL-OOD)
Across six datasets with unseen robots and viewpoints (976 trajectories in total), trajectory ranking consistency was evaluated using Kendall's $\tau_a$.

- **Main results**: RynnValue-8B achieves an average $\tau_a = 0.675$, surpassing Robometer (0.655), which was trained with full human preference supervision. Among preference-free methods, it substantially outperforms the prior best (0.502) and a progress-only baseline (0.292).
- **Instruction alignment**: Looking at instruction-trajectory matching matrices (Figure F3), RynnValue concentrates high values along the diagonal, achieving a normalized margin of 0.79 (compared to 0.67 for the best baseline). This confirms it responds specifically to task instructions rather than general motion intensity.
- **Ablations**: Removing temporal-order shuffling drops performance to 0.189, switching random sampling to uniform drops it to 0.379, and omitting Value-Isolation Attention lowers it to 0.482, demonstrating that shortcut prevention is crucial.

### 4.3 Scaling Law Analysis
The authors contrasted the impact of scaling episode counts within the same tasks versus expanding task diversity. Increasing episodes within fixed tasks quickly plateaued, whereas expanding task diversity drove steady error reductions. Heterogeneous task diversity is the primary driver of general value learning.

### 4.4 Case Study of Value Curves
Analyzing predicted trajectories on real robot runs (Figure F5), when the robot commits an error and moves away from the goal, Robometer remains flat, whereas RynnValue sharply drops its potential, immediately flagging the setback.

### 4.5 Real-World Robot Reinforcement Learning
Evaluated on four complex bimanual Franka manipulation tasks, including bread bagging and spatula steak serving (Figure F6):
- **Offline RL (IQL)**: Trained on mixed-quality datasets, RynnValue reaches an 82.5% success rate, well above behavior cloning SFT (23.8%) and Robometer (63.8%).
- **Online RL (DSRL)**: Tested in randomized unseen initial configurations, RynnValue attains 72.5% success, outperforming Robometer at 52.5%.

Accurate task understanding places high rewards on the diagonal. RynnValue achieves a diagonal margin of 0.79, displaying significantly cleaner task discrimination than baselines.
captions.F5: Comparison of value curves on a real-world trajectory. During a task regression highlighted in purple (where an error moves the robot away from the goal state), Robometer remains largely insensitive, whereas RynnValue exhibits a sharp value dip that captures the failure.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what's next: longer horizons and richer embodiments
sections.summary: By adopting temporal distance as supervision, RynnValue demonstrates how value foundation models can scale to massive datasets without preference labels. Future directions include handling longer time horizons, incorporating energy and safety metrics into value design, and expanding to five-finger hands and mobile manipulation.
sections.details:
This work presents a paradigm shift from normalized progress to temporal distance (cost-to-go) in robotic reward modeling. By supervising models with timestamp-derived temporal distance and eliminating structural shortcuts via shuffling and Value-Isolation Attention, it proves that heterogeneous large-scale data can be unified under a single value interface without preference annotations.

The authors highlight three main future directions:
- **Longer horizons and streaming inference**: The current setup operates on subsampled windows; extending this to long-horizon tasks and real-time streaming inference is a natural next step.
- **Richer value semantics**: The current model focuses on minimum-time control. Incorporating multi-faceted costs such as energy efficiency, safety margins, and manipulation precision into the value function would be valuable.
- **Expanding embodiments**: Applying the framework to high-degree-of-freedom dexterous hands and whole-body mobile manipulation presents promising avenues.

takeaways: For generalist robot reward models, temporal distance (cost-to-go) derived from timestamps has clearer physical grounding and scales far more cleanly than normalized progress.
Because multi-frame vision models readily exploit sequence order and temporal spacing shortcuts, sequence shuffling and Value-Isolation Attention are essential for robust learning.
To improve generalist reward foundation models, scaling task diversity is far more effective than simply collecting more episodes of existing tasks.
Using potential-based reward shaping, a pretrained temporal distance model can directly serve as an effective dense reward signal for both online and offline real-world robot RL.
limitations: Relying on a fixed-length (8-frame) subsampled window limits direct deployment to real-time streaming inference and ultra-long-horizon tasks.
Because it assumes minimum-time task execution, the model does not account for non-temporal costs like motion smoothness, safety margins, or energy consumption.
For contact-rich tasks requiring millimeter-level precision, such as tight drawer alignment, estimating value accurately from RGB images alone remains challenging.
